meters.label: Real effects reached by a test

frames.narration: An order service charges a card, sends an email and reads the clock. First version: it builds the real gateway, mailer and clock itself. A test of one checkout reaches all 3 real systems and cannot replace any.

Constructor injection: the service takes the three collaborators as parameters, and the composition root decides which ones. A test passes 3 fakes and reaches 0 real effects. The constructor shows what the class needs.

A test forgets the mailer fake. With constructor injection the service cannot be built: 'missing mailer', raised before the test body runs, with 0 real effects. In a compiled language it would not compile.

Service locator: the service asks a global registry. The constructor says nothing about needs. The same test registers two fakes, the locator still holds the real mailer, and the checkout runs and sends 1 real email with no warning.

A fourth dependency, a tax calculator, arrives with 4 existing tests. Constructor injection: 6 files edited, and the 4 tests fail to build until they pass a fake. The locator: 2 files edited, and the 4 tests quietly keep using the real calculator.

A container wires the graph from registrations. That is useful at scale. Taken to the extreme, every class is injected through an interface: nine collaborators, 9 fakes in each test, and 8 files for the fourth dependency, even though six of the nine are trivial helpers no test replaces.

Inject what varies or reaches outside the process, through the constructor, and wire it in one place. Call pure helpers directly. Treat a locator in domain code and a container that hides the graph as costs, not features.
